CREATORS.summary: Nobody in this era was hired to make advertisements. The agency was invented as a space broker: Volney B. Palmer opened in Philadelphia in 1841-42 and was paid by publishers, taking roughly 25 percent of what he sold. By the 1850s a dozen rivals each claimed to represent every paper of importance, and the commission an agent could extract ranged from about 10 to 50 percent. George P. Rowell (Boston, 1865) industrialised the model by buying space in bulk and reselling it in slices. The decisive break came in 1875, when N. W. Ayer & Son offered advertisers the 'open contract': the agent would work for the buyer, disclose the rate, and take a fixed percentage. Once the agent's income no longer depended on hiding the price, the agency had to sell something else - market research (Ayer's Nichols-Shepard study, 1880), then copy and art (from the 1890s). By 1904-07 Lord & Thomas under Albert Lasker had turned copy into the product, hiring John E. Kennedy ('advertising is salesmanship in print') and then Claude Hopkins, who tested headlines against keyed coupons. The full-service agency, the pitch, and the fixed commission all existed before 1917; the trade body that froze them, the 4As, was founded in June of that year.

BUYERS.summary: The first buyers of national advertising were patent-medicine makers. They had no shops, no salesmen and no repeat-purchase guarantee, so print was the entire business, and they were N. W. Ayer's most lucrative category in 1878 at 26 percent of agency revenue. Behind them came the branded packaged goods of the 1870s and 1880s (Heinz 1876, Ivory 1879, Quaker, Royal Baking Powder), whose problem was persuading a grocer's customer to ask for a name. A second, quite separate pool was retail: department stores (Macy's 1858, Wanamaker's 1876, Marshall Field's 1887) bought local newspaper space by the inch, and by 1915 local advertising was four times national in newspapers. A third pool was mail order - Montgomery Ward (1872) and Sears (1888) - which bought advertising strictly to produce measured orders and turned the catalogue itself into an advertising medium. The fourth pool was individuals and very small businesses buying classified lines over a newspaper counter, the only self-serve, no-agency channel in the era. The era's marginal new buyer class is the national brand manufacturer: the Association of National Advertisers was founded in 1910 in Detroit, and it was that advertiser bloc that forced audited circulation in 1914.

SELLERS.summary: The sellers were publishers, and they were extraordinarily fragmented: 22,754 newspapers and periodicals in 1914, of which 2,580 were dailies. Nobody held pricing power over a national audience, which is exactly why brokers could exist. The structural invention of the era belongs to the sell side, not the buy side. Benjamin Day's New York Sun (3 September 1833) sold at a penny - below cost - and said so on its own front page, promising readers cheap news and advertisers 'an advantageous medium'. Sixty years later Frank Munsey industrialised the same trade, cutting Munsey's Magazine from 25 cents to 10 cents in 1893 while McClure's launched at 15 cents and Cosmopolitan cut to 12.5 cents; the ten-cent magazine sold below production cost and let advertising make up the difference. The result is visible in the Census: by 1914 advertising supplied about 65 percent of newspaper gross income, against roughly 44 percent in 1879. Outside print, the sellers were bill posters (Associated Bill Posters' Association, 1891), streetcar-card concessionaires (Barron Collier controlled about three-quarters of the market by the mid-1900s), classified directory publishers (Donnelley, 1886) and the Post Office itself, which sold reach to catalogue houses at subsidised third-class rates.

MEDIUM.summary: Newspapers were the dominant medium and stayed so for the whole era: Census enumeration puts newspaper advertising receipts at $184.1 million in 1914 against $71.6 million for all other periodicals. Magazines were the emerging channel and the only genuinely national one - after 1893 the ten-cent monthlies gave a manufacturer a single buy that covered the country. Four channels the later century treats as separate categories already existed and must be tracked from here: classified advertising, sold by the line over a counter since the penny press; directories, after Reuben H. Donnelley's classified telephone directory of 1886; direct mail and catalogues, riding third-class postage that grew from 301 million pieces in 1880 toward six billion by 1930, boosted by Rural Free Delivery (1896) and Parcel Post (1913); and outdoor plus streetcar cards, standardised by the Associated Bill Posters' Association (1891) and the 24-sheet poster. Business, trade and farm papers sat inside the Census 'other periodicals' line. There was no broadcast, no directory audit, and no medium that could be bought as a single national impression.

SCALE.summary: There is no annual series for this era and none can honestly be built. The earliest quantitative estimate of US advertising volume is a Printers' Ink retrospective benchmark for 1867, carried into the Census Bureau's Historical Statistics of the United States as series T 444 and prepared by Robert J. Coen: $50m (1867), $200m (1880), $360m (1890), $542m (1900), $821m (1904), $1,142m (1909), $1,302m (1914), $1,627m (1917). Coen's own later revision, published in Advertising Age in 1999, runs 13-19 percent lower for the same years ($450m in 1900, $1,000m in 1909, $1,100m in 1914, $1,380m in 1917). Both lineages are carried here and the intervals widened rather than averaged. Nothing exists before 1867, so the 1840s-1866 stretch is an explicit no-data zone. The only A-grade anchor is the Census of Manufactures enumeration of newspaper and periodical advertising receipts ($202.5m in 1909, $255.6m in 1914, $528.2m in 1919), which runs three to five times below the benchmark totals because the census counts publisher receipts while the benchmark counts advertiser outlay including preparation and non-media promotion. GLOBAL FIGURE: an explicit absence. No global advertising expenditure estimate exists for any year before 1917; the earliest recurring international survey lineage begins with the International Advertising Association (founded 1938) and its later Starch INRA Hooper 'Survey of World Advertising Expenditures'. Searches of the statistical-compendium literature and the world-survey lineage returned nothing pre-1917.

claims.statement: The four money-type pools account for 62.2 percent of the 1914 benchmark, leaving 37.8 percent - about $454 million - unattributed. Roughly 5 to 9 points of that is a real fifth money type: business, trade and technical papers, legal, financial and government notices, and institutional and political money. The rest is the undocumented gap between a contemporaneous channel enumeration and a retrospective benchmark, and it is not a money type.
claims.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
claims.method: RECONCILIATION IS FORCED AND EXACT. The four pool medians sum to 62.2 percent of the $1,200m observed total (national brand 22.0 + local retail 22.0 + classified 2.2 + direct response 16.0), leaving 37.8 percent = $454m unattributed; 22.0 + 22.0 + 2.2 + 16.0 + 37.8 = 100.0 exactly. The residual is reported as its own figure, not absorbed. Lens centrals: structural-proxy 9.3, reference-class 34.8, decomposition 44.7. || IT DECOMPOSES INTO TWO PARTS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFLATED. PART ONE, roughly 5-9 points ($60-112m): a GENUINE FIFTH MONEY TYPE the four-way taxonomy cannot hold - business, trade and technical paper advertising (the Census other-periodicals class is about 28 percent business and technical papers, dealer- and engineer-directed money), dealer-directed direct mail, house organs, legal, financial and government notices in newspapers, theatrical and circus billposting, and institutional, transportation and political advertising. Two lenses sized it independently at 9.3 and 5.2 percent, and it is corroborated forward: Coen's business-papers line was $76m of a $1,690m total in 1935, or 4.5 percent, with legal and financial notices a further 2-4 percent of newspaper linage. This part is real money with a real name and should be a labelled series in any chart. PART TWO, roughly 29-33 points ($350-400m): a DENOMINATOR ARTEFACT, the gap between a contemporaneous channel enumeration and a retrospective benchmark that nobody has ever decomposed. It is not a money type and must never be drawn as one. || THE GAP'S SIZE AND WHY IT EXISTS. Two anchors exist for 1914 and they are 1.72x apart. The MEASURED base is $697-725m: the twelve Printers' Ink channels, which sum exactly to their stated $616m, grown to 1914 at the Census newspaper-receipts ratio x1.131 = $697m, plus window display and directory listings. It is independently corroborated by Starch 1914 p. 7 ('nearly $700,000,000 are spent annually' on printed advertising), and its newspaper line reproduces the documented 1.5187 receipts-to-outlay wedge to within 1.1 percent (1.5356 against 1.5187). The RETROSPECTIVE benchmark is $1,200m. The $503m difference is 42 percent of the denominator, and the SAME PUBLISHING HOUSE's contemporaneous 1911 tabulation runs 38-46 percent below its own retrospective series for adjacent years, with no documented reconciliation anywhere. || TWO READINGS, BOTH CARRIED, NEITHER AVERAGED AWAY. READING A: the gap is genuine cost of preparation and non-media promotion, which the HSUS source note for series T 444-471 says is inside the basis - in which case it IS buyer money and belongs to the pools, allocated by below-the-line intensity (national brand about 1.4x space money, local retail about 0.7x, direct response about 0.5x because its lines are already all-in, classified about 0.0x), and the residual collapses to the fifth pool alone at 5-9 percent. That is the structural-proxy lens's position and the source of the interval's lower bound of 5. READING B: the gap is retrospective overstatement in the Printers' Ink / Coen lineage, in which case it stays unallocated at 43-55 percent. That is the decomposition lens's position and the source of the upper bound of 55. The consolidated central sits between them, closer to B, because the median rejected the full allocation that only one of three lenses performed. || THE GAP CANNOT BE SPREAD EVENLY, and this is a positive finding rather than a caveat. The measured-base lines are not on a common basis with each other: newspapers, periodicals and out-of-home are SPACE-ONLY (about $467m of the $697m), while direct mail, mail-order, novelty, sampling, distributing and house organs are ALL-IN production figures (about $230m). Broadening the denominator lifts the space pools by roughly their own value again and barely moves the all-in pools. The direct-mail share path is the check that confirms it: direct mail was 10-12 percent of the total-outlay basis in 1920 and 16.7 percent in 1935, so it cannot have been 25-30 percent in 1914, which an even spread would require. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses (structural-proxy [5,18], reference-class [22,45], decomposition [33,55]). national_brand.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
national_brand.method: SOURCED BY: no source. No compiler in or out of the window states national advertising as a share of total US advertising for any year 1840s-1917. Five independent routes survive after collapsing near-duplicates. || R1 ANPA newspaper national share, re-based from space to outlay, WEIGHT 0.25. Input: ANPA 1915 national $55m against local-including-classified $220m, i.e. 20.0 percent of newspaper money; Census 1914 newspaper receipts $184.047m x the documented 1.5187 Galbi wedge = $279.5m of newspaper outlay. ADJUSTMENTS: deflate 1915 to 1914 at the Census newspaper-receipts growth rate of about 4.4 percent a year, direction down, size -5 percent; raise national's share of OUTLAY above its share of SPACE, because national money carried materially more preparation per dollar of space (plates and electrotypes cut once and shipped to hundreds of papers, agency art and copy), direction up, size +3pp. Result about 23 percent of newspaper outlay, about $64m. local_retail.statement: Local retail advertising, excluding classified, was about 22 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, roughly $264 million. It ties with national brand as the joint-largest money type, and every route that raises one mechanically lowers the other.
local_retail.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
local_retail.method: SOURCED BY: no source for the pool. The only in-window dollar figure is ANPA's newspaper local line, whose own column header says it INCLUDES classified ($220m in 1915), and no compiler has ever separated the two. Sourced inputs: ANPA via Borden via Galbi (third-hand); the Harvard Bureau of Business Research's measured advertising-to-net-sales ratios (grade A/B, in window, directly measured, but the retail-sales denominator they multiply is constructed). Grade stays C. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 36.4, reference-class 22, decomposition 22.0). No extremizing; shared evidence base. Three routes survive, one of them only half-independent. || L1 ANPA local line net of classified, plus local out-of-home, WEIGHT 0.40. Input: ANPA local-including-classified $220m for 1915; total newspaper outlay 1914 $279.5m (Census receipts x 1.5187); local shares of the PI 1911 out-of-home and promotion lines grown to 1914 (novelty about 50 percent, billposting about 35, outdoor 45-50, streetcar 22-40, theatre programmes about 70, distributing 50-75, plus 14-15 percent of the direct-mail line as merchants' circulars). PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the ANPA line is 1915 and bundles classified, and classified must be subtracted on a RECEIPTS basis rather than a linage basis. ADJUSTMENTS: deflate 1915 to 1914, direction down, size -8 percent; remove classified at about 12 percent of newspaper receipts, -$22m. Basis check performed: ANPA's implied total newspaper money for 1914 is about $262m against the Census-derived $279.5m, 6 percent apart, so the ANPA basis needs no re-scaling. NEAR-DUPLICATES COLLAPSED: all three lenses ran this same ANPA line; ONE route. || L2 Harvard expense ratios x retail sales, WEIGHT 0.40. Touches no ANPA input and no Printers' Ink input - the only genuinely clean second route in the era. Input: Harvard's measured ratios by trade; US retail sales 1914 constructed at $15.8-17.5bn from nominal GDP $36,831m x a retail-to-GDP ratio of 0.43-0.47 taken from the 1929 Census of Distribution. THREE PROXY-POPULATION GAPS, each adjusted. (a) Trade mix: Harvard's spread across trades is an order of magnitude, so a single blended ratio is indefensible; trade-weighting food 28-30 percent at 0.15-0.2 percent, general merchandise 11-14 percent at 3.0 percent, apparel and shoes 10-13 percent at 2.0 percent, drug, furniture and hardware about 15 percent at 1.5-3.0 percent, automotive 7-10 percent at 0.8-1.2 percent, remainder at 0.5-1.0 percent gives 1.0-1.23 percent weighted, well below a naive blend. (b) Population: Harvard measures RETAIL STORES only, while the money type also holds local services - theatres and amusements, banks, hotels and restaurants, real-estate brokers, physicians, undertakers; direction up, size +15 to +30 percent. (c) Basis: the Harvard ratio is BOOKED advertising expense and already includes the store's own preparation, window trim and circulars, so it is comparable to the outlay basis and must NOT be scaled by the 1.5187 receipts wedge; applying the wedge here would double-count. KNOWN WEAKNESS CARRIED, NOT HIDDEN: Barger (NBER 1955), the correct retail-sales source, was located but not opened by any lens, and no in-window Harvard department-store bulletin exists, so importing a 1920s department-store ratio biases this route up. || L3 reference-class local-advertising-to-retail-sales ratio at 1935 and 1950, WEIGHT 0.20, HALF-INDEPENDENT. Input: Coen local 1935 $830m less about $90m classified = $740m against about $33bn of retail sales = 2.2 percent; Coen local 1950 $2,440m less $377m classified = $2,063m against about $145bn = 1.4 percent. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: 1935 is a depression year with a collapsed sales denominator, which inflates the ratio, so 1950 is the cleaner reading. ADJUSTMENT: band 1.3-1.7 percent applied to the same $17bn 1914 retail-sales figure L2 uses. DECLARED NOT INDEPENDENT: L3 shares L2's constructed denominator, so L2 and L3 are one-and-a-half routes, not two, and their agreement is partly mechanical. || THE KEY CROSS-CHECK: L1 and L2 share no input at all - one runs through ANPA newspaper dollars, the other through retailer profit and loss ratios on retail sales - and they land within 5-22 percent of each other in every lens that ran both. That is the strongest independent convergence in era 1 and it is what caps this pool. It also rejects a naive reference-class projection: carrying Coen's 1935 local share of 48.3 percent straight back would put local at about $580m, which requires a blended advertising-to-sales ratio above 2 percent that the Harvard grocery bulletin directly contradicts. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the three lenses. The structural-proxy lens's 36.4 comes from the same below-the-line denominator treatment described under e1-scale-011, not from a different measurement of the money.

classified.statement: Classified advertising was about 2.2 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, about $26 million. It was the smallest of the four money types by a wide margin, and that is the one ordering this era can honestly assert.
classified.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
classified.method: SOURCED BY: NO SOURCE FOUND, and this is a documented negative result rather than an unfinished search. No compiler published a classified dollar figure, a classified share or a classified linage series for any year 1840s-1917. Exhausted: the Census of Manufactures printing and publishing bulletins 1879-1919 (receipts enumerated but never split by class of advertising); HSUS T 485-491 and Millennial De516-522 (both start 1928, both sourced to Media Records Inc., trademark filed November 1928); Coen via Galbi (no classified category ever, no national/local partition before 1935); ANCAM (founded 1920); PIB (1945); SRDS (1919, and it publishes rates not spend); NAA (1950 onward); the Library of Congress inventory of historical marketing data (nothing pre-1919); and Printers' Ink 4 May 1911, which has NO classified line among its twelve channels. The best in-window evidence is firm-level and about LINAGE: Field 1916 on the Chicago Tribune. Grade C, and it cannot be raised by further search. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 2.2, reference-class 2.2, decomposition 2.4) - the tightest agreement in the panel, reached from three different route mixes. Four routes survive after collapsing near-duplicates, plus one correction all three lenses made independently. || C1 Media Records 52-city linage band, back-projected and universe-adjusted, WEIGHT 0.30. Input: HSUS T 485-486 - classified was 18-21 percent of newspaper linage in 52 cities in EVERY year 1928-1941 (1928 19.2 percent, 1930 18.1, 1933 18.5, 1936 19.2, 1938 20.8, 1940 20.7), a band that held through a 44 percent collapse in total linage. TWO PROXY-POPULATION GAPS, both adjusted downward. (a) Period: the series starts eleven years after the window, and help-wanted, used-automobile and suburban-real-estate classified all expanded in the 1920s (motor registrations rose roughly tenfold 1915-29); direction down, size small and poorly evidenced, and partly offset by the band's stability through the Depression. (b) Universe: the 52-city panel is metropolitan, while the 1914 universe was 2,580 dailies among 22,754 publications and far more weekly-heavy. ADJUSTMENT: if metro papers carried about 60 percent of newspaper money at 19-25 percent classified and small papers ran 8-12 percent, the national average is about 15-19 percent of linage; direction down, size -3.8pp, LARGER than the period adjustment and pointing the same way. || C2 Chicago Tribune 1916 scaled by a calibrated top-paper-to-average ratio, WEIGHT 0.20. Input: Field 1916, about 50 percent of linage at the country's leading want-ad daily. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the Tribune is the extreme upper tail of a distribution whose mean is the quantity wanted. ADJUSTMENT: calibrate the top-paper-to-average ratio on the one year where both exist in the same measurement tradition - the 52-city average was 19.2 percent in 1928 while leading want-ad papers ran near 50 percent, a ratio of 2.0-2.5x - then apply it in reverse to Field's 50 percent, then apply C1's small-paper universe adjustment; direction down, size -60 percent from the raw figure. Result about 16 percent of national linage in 1916, landing on C1 from a wholly different and IN-WINDOW source. That two independent traditions converge at 15-16 percent of linage is this pool's strongest result. || C3 linage-to-receipts rate conversion calibrated on the NAA 1950 revenue identity, WEIGHT 0.20. Input: NAA 1950 newspaper revenue - national $518m, retail $1,175m, classified $377m of $2,070m, so classified was 18.2 percent of newspaper REVENUE in 1950; Rogers 1918 prints a two-cents-per-word classified rate. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the rate ratio r (classified revenue per agate line over display revenue per agate line) is the single unmeasured hinge and no source in or out of the window states it. ADJUSTMENT: solve revenue_share = L*r/(L*r + (1-L)) for r at the plausible 1950 classified linage share of 22-27 percent, which yields r = 0.60-0.79, far above the naive metropolitan rate-card comparison of 0.3-0.4, for two structural reasons - classified is set solid with no white space so every agate line is paid words, and classified carried no 15 percent agency commission and no contract discount. Use r = 0.70 (band 0.55-0.90). Applying it to a 15-19 percent linage share gives 11-14 percent of newspaper receipts. || C4 transaction-count Fermi, WEIGHT 0.20. Shares no input with any linage or revenue series - the only fully independent route here. Input: about 20.5m US households of which about 10m urban; urban households placing want ads, 30 percent of 10m at 2 orders = 6m; employers placing help-wanted against very high period labour turnover, 500,000 firms at 6 a year = 3m; landlords, rooming-house keepers and real-estate agents, 1m at 4 a year = 4m; lost-and-found, personals, business opportunity, livestock and agents-wanted 3m; about 16m orders at a blended $1.50. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the two-cents-per-word rate is a metropolitan card, so small-town rates bias the average order value DOWN while a roughly 10 percent tail of standing dealer, agency and rooming-house contracts at about $8 biases it UP, the second being the larger term. Result 13.0 percent of newspaper receipts. || C5 newspaper-total reconciliation residual, WEIGHT 0.10, upper bound only. Forces newspaper outlay $279.5m less national about $64m less local-retail newspaper display (from the independent L2 build, $150-180m), bracketing classified at $36-66m of newspaper money on a space basis. || THE CORRECTION ALL THREE LENSES MADE INDEPENDENTLY, and the most consequential result of this pass: the documented 1.5187 Coen-to-Census wedge must NOT be applied to classified. That wedge is agency commission plus cost of preparation, and classified was the era's one channel with neither - no agency, no plates, no copy, no position charges, cash over a counter, with Rogers 1918 carrying 'Expenses, Classified' as its own sub-ledger. Classified outlay therefore equals classified receipts, so classified's share of OUTLAY sits BELOW its share of RECEIPTS (about 13 percent of receipts maps to about 8 percent of newspaper outlay), which REVERSES the direction of the adjustment the superseded reading applied. The corollary the chapter should carry: the wedge is ASYMMETRIC by money type - above 1.5187 for national brand (implied display-only wedge about 1.58), roughly 1.15-1.25 for local retail placed direct with the paper, and 1.00 for classified. Directory and telephone classified listings are carried at $3-4m (band $2-8m) as this pool's only non-newspaper component. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses. Its width is driven by two treatment levers, not by measurement: the rate ratio r (0.55-0.90) and the wedge treatment. The upper bound of 5.0 is what classified becomes if a future pass rejects the no-wedge argument and applies the full 1.5187 factor.

direct_response.statement: Direct-response money - catalogues, direct mail, and keyed print space bought by mail-order houses and patent-medicine makers - was about 16 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, roughly $192 million. It cannot be ranked against national brand or local retail.
direct_response.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
direct_response.method: SOURCED BY: PARTIAL, and materially better sourced than the superseded record. Printers' Ink of 4 May 1911 p. 79 publishes the component channels IN WINDOW and CONTEMPORANEOUSLY - direct mail $100m, farm and mail-order $75m, demonstration and sampling $18m, distributing $6m, house organs $7m - and that sourced tabulation supersedes the 1926 Britannica back-cast as this pool's primary anchor. The POOL still grades C for two reasons recorded at source and not resolvable: no source in the era uses the term 'direct response', so assigning these channels to it is interpretation; and the $75m 'farm and mail-order' line does not say how much is space bought in farm and mail-order journals (a medium) versus advertising placed by mail-order houses (a money type) - a $0-85m swing. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 16.0, reference-class 19, decomposition 14.0). No extremizing; shared evidence base. All three lenses moved this pool DOWN, for two named mechanical reasons rather than one judgment. Four routes survive after collapsing near-duplicates, plus one binding ceiling. || D1 Printers' Ink 1911 direct lines re-based to 1914, WEIGHT 0.35. Input: the five channels above, grown x1.131 to 1914 - direct mail $113m, farm and mail-order $85m, sampling $20m, distributing $7m, house organs $8m. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: direct mail in 1914 was not one money type; it carried consumer order-seeking mail, manufacturers' dealer and trade literature, and local merchants' house-to-house circulars. ADJUSTMENT: split 65 percent direct response, 20 percent business-to-business, 15 percent local retail, with the 50-80 percent range on that first share the single largest lever in this pool; house organs are predominantly dealer- and employee-directed, take 40 percent; sampling is largely national-brand trial generation rather than order-seeking, take 15-30 percent. || D2 mail-order sales x expense ratio, WEIGHT 0.30. Input: Sears about $101m of sales in 1914, Montgomery Ward about $45m; the two at 40-45 percent of the trade implies total US mail-order sales of $325-365m; the all-in advertising ratio for a mail-order house runs 8-14 percent of sales against store retail's about 1.1 percent, because the catalogue IS the store. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: no source states a mail-order advertising ratio, so it is validated rather than assumed - Sears's four-pound, 1,200-page big book at roughly $0.40-0.60 a copy over 15-20m mailed pieces a year gives $7.5-12m, i.e. 8-12 percent of sales, which reproduces the ratio from physical production arithmetic. ADJUSTMENT: apply 8-14 percent to $325-365m of trade sales. PARTIAL DEPENDENCE DECLARED: one lens's version of this route also leans on a Printers' Ink-derived residual, so only the sales-ratio half is clean; the clean half reproduces that residual ($48.3m against $48.0m) from a wholly different derivation, which is what resolves the farm-and-mail-order break toward mail-order houses' own outlay. || D3 Britannica 1920 back-cast, WEIGHT 0.15. Input: the 1926 Encyclopaedia Britannica's direct mail 'about $300,000,000' for 1920. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: six years past the era close, retrospective and tertiary. ADJUSTMENTS: deflate for the price level, CPI roughly doubled 1914-1920 (30.1 to 60.0, x1.99), direction down; deflate for real growth, +15 to +25 percent of real expansion over 1914-20 boosted by Liberty Loan and war-agency mail, direction down. $300m / (1.99 x 1.20) = about $126m for 1914, against D1's $113m, 12 percent apart. The value of running this route is not its estimate but its retirement: it shows the two anchors are mutually consistent and removes the record's reliance on the back-cast as primary. || D4 direct-mail share-of-total path across four observations, WEIGHT 0.20 - THE DISCRIMINATING ROUTE. Input: direct mail as a share of each compiler's own total - 16.2 percent in the PI 1911 table (100/616), 10.2-12.1 percent in 1920 (Coen $2,480m over HSUS $2,935m), 16.4 percent in 1935 (HSUS T 464 $282m over T 444 $1,690m), 14.1 percent in 1950 (Coen $803m of $5,700m). PROXY-POPULATION GAP: each share sits on its own compiler's denominator, and the pre-1919 denominator is not like-for-like with the post-1935 one. ADJUSTMENT: the observed path pins Coen-basis direct mail at 10-12 percent of the 1914 total, i.e. $120-144m, only 6-27 percent above the contemporaneous PI line, because the PI direct-mail and mail-order lines are ALREADY all-in production-plus-postage figures and barely scale when the basis broadens, while pure space money scales by roughly its own value again. This is the only route that constrains how the measured base maps onto the broad benchmark, and it rests on observed post-window readings rather than judgment: an even spread of the $503m basis gap would require a direct-mail line far above 12 percent of the total and CONTRADICTS the observed 1920 and 1935 readings. || THE BINDING CEILING (a constraint, not a route, WEIGHT 0). Adams, Collier's, 7 October 1905, put total US consumer spending on patent medicines at $75m. Grown to about $110m of retail by 1914, with manufacturers taking about 55 percent and spending about 40 percent of that on advertising, the ENTIRE patent-medicine category's advertising of every kind cannot exceed roughly $25-33m, of which only the keyed and mail-order portion is direct response. The superseded reading assigned $30-50m to patent-medicine KEYED PRESS ALONE. Caveat carried: Adams's $75m is a round number in a polemic, and at $200m of real retail spending the ceiling relaxes and this pool rises 2-3 points. || WHY THE POOL FELL. Two named mechanical causes, not a judgment call. (1) Double counting: the superseded method added mail-order and patent-medicine KEYED PRESS on top of a direct-mail base, but that keyed space is already inside the newspaper and periodical lines counted in the other pools; it also added premiums, samples and novelties wholesale, which the PI channel table places largely with national brand and local retail (novelty $30m was mostly local-merchant giveaway, sampling $18m mostly national-brand trial generation). Worth 4-5 points. (2) The patent-medicine ceiling above, worth 2-3 points. The basis correction is separate from and additional to both. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses.

PRICING.summary: Price was set by the publisher's rate card, quoted per agate line or per inch, and then quietly unset by everyone. Because circulation was unverifiable, the card price was an asking price: publishers 'never held to their stated prices' and agents bid each other down, with commissions of anywhere between 10 and 50 percent of the space price flowing back to whoever placed the order. Two mechanisms fixed this. The first was Ayer's open contract (1875), which put the agent on the buyer's side and made the commission a disclosed, fixed percentage; that rate drifted experimentally and stabilised at 15 percent by the early 1890s. The second was enforcement: Curtis Publishing's no-rebating rule (1891) and the newspaper publishers' 1893 resolution to pay commission only to 'recognised' agents, never to advertisers, turned the 15 percent into a cartel price that survived until the 1990s. The third leg was verification. Once the Audit Bureau of Circulations (1914) certified the circulation a rate card was based on, the card became a contract term rather than an opening bid. Take rate in this era: the agency took 15 percent of gross billings, and the publisher kept the rest. Classified was priced separately and simply - a flat rate per line, no position charges, no plates, no agency.

claims.statement: Before standardisation, the commission an agent received on advertising space varied between about 10 and 50 percent of the space price.

Fifteen percent was customary from the early 1890s and enforced from 1893 by publisher recognition; its industry-wide standardisation by the 4As is a 1918 act (era 2). The agency commission was the principal but not demonstrably the only intermediary cut: publishers also paid national special representatives, whose rate is not established here.

MEASUREMENT.summary: The counted thing was circulation, and for most of the era nobody counted it honestly. Publishers stated their own figures, and advertisers had no way to test them, which is why the rate card was unenforceable. The first counting institution was commercial: George P. Rowell's American Newspaper Directory (1869) listed 5,778 US papers with Rowell's own estimated circulations, and N. W. Ayer's American Newspaper Annual followed in 1880. Advertisers then tried to police publishers themselves through the Association of American Advertisers, which folded in 1913. Government moved next: the Newspaper Publicity Act of 24 August 1912 made the cheap second-class mailing rate conditional on filing a sworn statement of ownership and, for daily papers, sworn circulation, and required paid reading matter to be labelled as advertisement; the Supreme Court upheld it in Lewis Publishing Co. v. Morgan (1913). The institutional climax came in 1914, when the publisher-backed Advertising Audit Association and the advertiser-backed Bureau of Verified Circulations merged in Chicago to form the Audit Bureau of Circulations, the world's first third-party media audit, promising 'facts without opinions' and empowered to suspend members that padded their numbers. Members filed statements twice a year and were audited once a year. Who paid the counter matters: ABC was funded jointly by advertisers, agencies and publishers, a tripartite model every later audit currency copied. Alongside it ran a second, private measurement tradition - the keyed coupon of mail order, which counted replies rather than readers.

claims.statement: Rowell's American Newspaper Directory, first issued in 1869, listed 5,778 American papers with estimated circulations, the first attempt at a common currency for buying space.

sources.name: Wikipedia, 'George P. Rowell'

TARGETING.summary: Targeting in this era meant choosing a publication and a place, not choosing a person. The unit of precision was the title: a farm weekly reached farmers, a religious paper reached churchgoers, Ladies' Home Journal reached women who kept house, a city daily reached one city. Rowell's directory and Ayer's annual existed precisely to let a buyer sort 5,778 and then 22,754 titles by geography and character. A second, sharper form of precision came from the mail: catalogue houses and direct-mail advertisers addressed named individuals on lists, and Rural Free Delivery (1896) plus Parcel Post (1913) made rural households reachable and servable - Sears filled five times as many orders in 1913 as in 1912. The sharpest precision of all was self-selection. Classified advertising let a reader who already wanted a job, a room or a horse go to the column where those offers sat, which is intent-matching by category, done by hand; the classified telephone directory (Donnelley, 1886) put the same idea on a shelf. Response measurement was the era's substitute for audience data: Claude Hopkins at Lord & Thomas keyed each coupon to its publication and headline, so a mail-order advertiser could rank titles by cost per reply while a soap advertiser could rank nothing at all.

claims.statement: The buyer's targeting menu grew from 5,778 listed newspapers in 1869 to 22,754 enumerated newspapers and periodicals in 1914, a fourfold increase in selectable audience units.

events.title: The penny press invents ad-subsidised content
events.desc: Benjamin Day launched the New York Sun at one cent, below the cost of production, and printed the model on his own front page: to lay the news before the public 'at a price within the means of every one, and at the same time offer an advantageous medium for advertisements'. Within about two years he was selling roughly 15,000 copies a day. Every later ad-funded free service - broadcast radio, network television, the portal, search - is a rerun of this trade.

claim.statement: The New York Sun sold at one cent and reached roughly 15,000 copies a day within about two years of its 1833 launch.

sources.name: Wikipedia, 'The Sun (New York City)'
The Founding of the Penny Press (ERIC ED360650)

events.title: Volney Palmer opens as a space broker
events.desc: Palmer set up in Philadelphia as a newspaper agent, paid by publishers with a commission widely reported at 25 percent of the space he sold. Sources split on the year: the Pennsylvania Center for the Book dates the agency to 1841, while Horsky and Zeithammer date it to 1842 from an 1846 newspaper notice. The record treats him as the first or among the first US advertising agents rather than asserting a clean superlative.

events.title: Montgomery Ward mails the first mail-order list
events.desc: Ward mailed a single page listing 163 items to members of the Grange. It grew to 72 pages by 1874 and nearly 1,000 pages by 1897, supporting about $7 million of annual sales. Mail order is where advertising first became measurable: every dollar of catalogue and keyed print advertising was judged by orders received, and that accounting tradition runs unbroken to the click.

claim.statement: Montgomery Ward's first mail-order catalogue, 1872, was a single page listing 163 items.

sources.name: United States Postal Service, 'Advertising Mail: A Brief History'
WTTW Chicago Stories, 'The Rise and Fall of Chicago's Mail Order Giants'

events.title: N. W. Ayer's open contract switches the agent's side
events.desc: Ayer offered advertisers a long-term contract in which the advertiser supplied a budget rather than a media order, the agent bought whatever space he judged best, and the agent was paid a disclosed fixed percentage of the list price agreed among publisher, agent and advertiser. The first client was the rose grower Dingee & Conard. This is the moment the middleman stops working for the seller and starts working for the buyer, and it is what forced agencies to invent research, copy and art as their product.

events.title: Ladies' Home Journal refuses patent-medicine advertising
events.desc: Edward Bok announced that the Journal would accept no more patent-medicine advertisements, giving up a major revenue line. Seven other newspapers and periodicals followed within two years. This is the first documented case of a seller restricting its own inventory on trust grounds, and the opening move in the fight that produced the Pure Food and Drug Act.

events.title: The ten-cent magazine and the recognition rule
events.desc: Two mechanism changes land in one year. Frank Munsey cut Munsey's Magazine from 25 cents to 10 cents while McClure's launched at 15 cents and Cosmopolitan cut to 12.5 cents, making it possible to sell a magazine below its cost of production and let advertisers pay the difference; the ten-cent magazine grew the magazine-buying public from about 250,000 to 750,000 people by 1899. In the same year the newspaper publishers' association resolved that commissions would be paid only to recognised advertising agents and never to advertisers - the enforcement rule that turned a customary 15 percent into a cartel price.

claim.statement: Frank A. Munsey estimated that the ten-cent magazine grew the US magazine-buying public from about 250,000 to about 750,000 people between 1893 and 1899. This is the estimate of an interested party - the publisher who created the ten-cent magazine - and no independent measurement of the magazine-buying public exists for these years.

sources.name: Britannica, 'History of publishing: The 19th century and the start of mass circulation'
Encyclopedia.com, 'Munsey's Magazine' (for the corroborating Munsey's circulation path)

claim.method: Self-reported estimate by Frank A. Munsey, carried in the standard magazine histories. No independent enumeration exists; the interval is widened downward to allow for the promotional interest of the estimator, in the same way the record treats Palmer's self-reported newspaper count. Corroborating order of magnitude: Munsey's own circulation reached 500,000 by 1895 and 700,000 by 1897, so a total ten-cent magazine public of several hundred thousand to roughly a million is plausible.

events.title: 'The Great American Fraud' and the Pure Food and Drug Act
events.desc: Samuel Hopkins Adams began his Collier's Weekly series on 7 October 1905, showing that the leading cure-alls were alcohol, opiates and poisons, and naming the newspapers that carried them. Congress passed the Pure Food and Drug Act in 1906, prohibiting the manufacture, sale or transport of adulterated or misbranded drugs. The industry's biggest single advertiser category was regulated out of its old form, and advertising's own legitimacy became the trade's central problem.

events.title: Truth in advertising becomes law
events.desc: Printers' Ink retained counsel to draft a model statute criminalising false advertising on a strict-liability basis; states adopted it steadily, 22 in substantially the original form and 15 in modified form by November 1921. The Associated Advertising Clubs of America adopted the first formalised US advertising code the same year and ran vigilance committees that became the Better Business Bureaus. In August 1912 the Newspaper Publicity Act followed, conditioning the cheap second-class mail rate on sworn ownership and, for dailies, sworn circulation, and requiring paid reading matter to be marked as advertising; the Supreme Court upheld it in Lewis Publishing Co. v. Morgan (1913).

claim.statement: By November 1921 the Printers' Ink model statute had been adopted in 22 states in substantially its original form and in 15 more states in modified form.

sources.name: 1926 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Advertising' (Wikisource)
Hoofnagle, 'On the Printers' Ink Model Statute' (UC Berkeley Law)

events.title: Audited circulation and a federal regulator arrive together
events.desc: Advertisers, agencies and publishers merged two rival auditing bodies in Chicago in May 1914 to create the Audit Bureau of Circulations - the world's first third-party media audit, promising 'facts without opinions' and able to suspend members that padded circulation. The Federal Trade Commission Act was signed the same year, and the FTC brought its first deceptive-advertising case in 1916. From 1914 a rate card rests on a number somebody else checked, which is what makes it enforceable. Every later currency - ratings, impressions, the audited click - copies this tripartite, industry-funded design.

events.title: The agencies incorporate their cartel
events.desc: The American Association of Advertising Agencies was founded in St. Louis by five regional groups with 111 charter members. A year later, in 1918, the 4As standardised agency compensation at 15 percent of the gross space rate - a figure its own members described as reflecting their 1918 cost of doing business. The era closes with the middleman's price fixed, the audience audited, and the advertiser's money flowing through a recognised, screened, self-regulating layer.

boundary_notes: Handoff to era 2 (1918-1949). (1) SCALE lineages: the same two conflicting series continue across the boundary. Historical Statistics series T 444 gives 1918 $1,468m and 1919 $2,282m; Coen's 1999 revision gives 1918 $1,240m and 1919 $1,930m, about 15 percent lower, and Galbi's revision table shows that 15-18 percent gap persisting through 1929. Era 2 should carry both lineages for 1919-1934 and note that Coen's annual by-medium detail is only solid from 1935. The pre-1919 benchmarks are on a broader 'total outlay' basis (they include the cost of preparation and non-media promotion), so any chart splicing era 1 to era 2 must say so. (2) The constraint's '~$3B early 1900s' upper anchor is reached in 1920 ($2,935m in series T 444), not before 1917; the 1880 anchor of $200m is confirmed exactly. (3) A-grade print anchor at the boundary: Census of Manufactures advertising receipts for 1919 were $528.2m in total - newspapers $373.5m, other periodicals $154.8m - against $255.6m in 1914. Era 2's opening print level should reconcile with these. (4) The 15 percent commission: it stabilised as customary practice by the early 1890s and was enforced from 1893 by publisher recognition, but the industry-wide standardisation at 15 percent of the gross space rate is a 1918 act of the 4As, inside era 2. Era 2 owns the formalisation; era 1 owns the origin. (5) Measurement currency: ABC (1914) is the inherited currency and is print-only. Radio arrives in era 2 with no currency at all until Crossley/CAB in 1930, which is why sponsorship rather than spot pricing was the only workable mechanism at first. (6) Category continuity: classified, directories (Donnelley 1886), and direct mail all pre-date 1918 and must appear as tracked categories in era 2, not as later inventions; direct mail outlay was already about $300m in 1920. (7) Bookend for era 6: the classified counter and the mail-order coupon were this era's self-serve, no-agency, response-measured buying channels, bought by individuals and small businesses who never touched the 15 percent commission - the buyer class AdWords re-created. (8) Myth flags carried forward: the Wanamaker 'half my advertising' line is an attributed legend, earliest full attribution a 1919 sermon by Rev. Roy L. Smith with a partial, unattributed 1890 Printers' Ink antecedent; no primary Wanamaker source exists. The 'first advertising agency' superlative for Palmer is hedged (1841 or 1842 depending on source). (9) Global market size: no estimate of world advertising expenditure exists for any year in this era; the earliest recurring global survey lineage starts with the International Advertising Association (founded 1938). (10) Ad/GDP cross-era flag for the capture thread: era 2 records 3.0 percent of GDP in 1922 as the maximum of the entire 1919-2007 Coen/BEA series. Era 1's benchmark ratios reach a comparable or higher level earlier - roughly 3.1-3.5 percent in 1909 and 3.0-3.5 percent in 1914 - but they are NOT comparable to the 1919+ readings: the era-1 numerator is a broader total-outlay concept and the pre-1929 GDP denominator is a Johnston-Williamson reconstruction, not BEA national accounts. Both facts are correct as stated within their own windows. The chapter must not draw a single ad/GDP line across 1917-1919 without saying this.
